1:
Henry reads the search as a trap that failed. The adversaries appealed to the decree because the Jews had pleaded it, perhaps hoping it would not be found; and the tribes, having kept no copy, had to fall back on the original. It was looked for in Babylon, where Cyrus had signed it, and when it was not there Darius refused to treat the absence as proof that no decree existed, and had other repositories searched. Delitzsch supposes the Babylon search itself turned up the information that documents from the time of Cyrus were kept in the fortress at Achmetha, where the roll was then found. Gill makes the order an inquiry after the edict among the public records; Wesley traces the two stages, Babylon first and Achmetha after. Ellicott corrects two words: the king gave an order rather than made a decree, and the treasures were laid down rather than laid up, in a chamber for storing documents and valuables. Clarke renders the house of the rolls the house of the books, that is the king's library, and remarks that this is the first time we hear of a library at all.

Where Achmetha was, and why the roll lay there, they settle between them. Gill reports that two Jewish commentators took the word for a vessel in which writings were kept, rejects that for a place-name, follows the Vulgate and Josephus in reading Ecbatana, and explains that the Persian kings wintered at Shushan and summered in Media, the city taking its name from heat, so that one writer compared them to cranes for their passages. Clarke and Wesley agree on the summer residence and the royal city of the Medes and Persians, Clarke adding that Cyrus's records had probably all been carried there. Delitzsch gives the fullest account: the capital of Great Media built by Dejokes, a summer residence of Persian and Parthian kings near the modern Hamadan, with Achmetha the Old-Median form of the name. Ellicott alone explains why a copy and not the original was found: the parchment was probably destroyed at Babylon by Smerdis, and what survived here was a transcript. Henry suspects instead that someone unwilling to destroy the decree had hidden it out of ill will, that the Jews might lose its benefit, and that Providence brought it to light.

Henry sorts the decree into three warrants, for the building with its dimensions and materials, for the expenses out of the royal revenue, and for the restoring of the vessels, the priests to return them each to its place; of the second he notes that the money seems never to have arrived, the face of things at court being soon changed. The dimensions trouble two voices. Clarke measures the new house against the old and finds it much the larger, sixty cubits each way against twenty broad and thirty high, and has the courses of stone alternating with timber carried up to the square of the building. Wesley will not have the comparison stand so: either Solomon's were sacred cubits and these common ones, or the sixty cubits of height belong to the porch only, and the word rendered breadth may mean extension or length, since a king would hardly prescribe one dimension and leave the other unsaid. On the materials Gill passes on the reading that makes the three rows the walls and the great stones marble. Clarke observes that Cyrus had timber cut at Libanus and brought to Joppa at his own charge and furnished the sacrifices, but the Jews paid the rest. Ellicott notes that the decree strengthens the prophecy of a laid foundation with a word meaning sufficiently supported, and reads the return of the vessels as expiation for Belshazzar's profaning of them, every word emphatic down to the twice-repeated house of God; Delitzsch adds that the singular verb is distributive, each vessel to its own place.
6:
Ellicott marks the abrupt turn into the words of the decree itself, and allows that its terms were either drawn up with Jewish help or rendered freely into the national phraseology by the historian. Delitzsch adds that the answer was undoubtedly sent to the governor in writing, though the historian gives the contents without saying so. The opening command is a warning off rather than a permission: Ellicott glosses it as keeping aloof from interference of any kind, Clarke turns it positive, that the officers further the work rather than interrupt it. Gill hears in the phrasing a suspicion that they meant to molest the builders, or that others were urging them to it. He places the governor on the Israel side of the Euphrates and passes on the description of him as master of the horse, and he parts company with Josephus on the next clause, taking it for an additional decree granting more than Cyrus had where Josephus makes it a confirmation of the earlier one. Ellicott adds that the money was to come from tribute already collected for Persia, deducted before remittance, and Delitzsch that the phrase forbidding hindrance means the work is not to be discontinued.

The provision for sacrifice is what surprises its readers. Ellicott calls the list of bullocks, rams and lambs an account accurate enough to be checked against the law itself, and notes that the word rendered appointment simply means direction. He finds two ends served, the honouring of the God of heaven and the interceding of the Jews for the dynasty, and argues from the one other occurrence of the phrase for sweet savours that incense is meant here too, which shows under what good instruction the decree was drawn. Delitzsch takes the longer view: Cyrus had ordered the rebuilding because he owned the God of Israel as the God of heaven who gave him his kingdoms, and Darius walks in his footsteps, wanting that blessing on his own house. Such an acknowledgment, he insists, cost a Persian king nothing in principle, since he might honour Jahve as the mightiest God of heaven without being unfaithful to the gods of his fathers. Clarke draws out the policy rather than the theology: even heathens believed offerings made on their behalf to the God of the Jews would avail, and the same calculation has moved established religions to tolerate other forms for the benefit of their prayers.

The sanction draws comment on its words and its parallels. Gill makes altering the word mean acting contrary to it, revoking it so far as one may. Ellicott prefers violating the command outright, since the alteration of a Persian decree was a thing unheard of, and reports that the penalty named is literally crucifixion, which among the Persians generally meant nailing a body to a cross after decapitation and among the Assyrians impalement. Clarke is less sure which punishment is meant, canvassing hanging, gibbeting and whipping at a post before settling on empaling, and reads the ruin of the offender's house as rubble never used again but for the most sordid purposes. Delitzsch separates the saying from its substance: the clause about the God who has caused his name to dwell there is Israelitish and must have come from the Jewish historian, but what it asks, that God himself destroy whoever injures the temple, is how the great Persian inscription at Bisitun closes, imprecating the judgments of Ahuramazda on any who deface the image and the writing and invoking blessing on those who respect them. Gill reads the same clause of the Shechinah dwelling as in Solomon's temple, which he thinks Darius knew of; and Wesley turns the curse forward, that the temple was at length justly destroyed by God's own hand, yet perhaps the Romans who were the instruments of it felt the curse too, their empire declining ever after until it was destroyed itself.
13:
Henry makes the reversal the point: the men who had come in haste to stop the work now came in as much haste to help it, did what the king ordered and did it speedily so as not to be thought grudging, and were made moderate by the king's moderation against their own inclination. The elders then built cheerfully, and for all he can tell with their own hands. Gill notes only that the governor had read the letter and the builders went on. On the date the sources are careful and not quite agreed. Gill fixes Adar as the twelfth month, answering to part of February and part of March; Ellicott makes it the last month of the ecclesiastical year and reckons the work from its resumption, which the prophet dates exactly, at four years five months and ten days, though twenty-one years had passed since the foundation was first laid; Clarke, dating by years of the world, puts the sixth year of Darius twenty years after Zerubbabel laid it under Cyrus. Delitzsch keeps the clause that governs it all, that they built and finished according to the commandment of the God of Israel and the command of the kings.

Those kings, named together, raise a difficulty nobody evades. Delitzsch states it plainly: a predecessor of Darius cannot be meant by a name that follows his, so the third must be Artaxerxes Longimanus, who reigned long after the temple was finished. Ellicott takes the verse as a summary of every agent in the work, from the first king to the last, with the elders and the prophets named too but everything traced to the God of Israel whose commandment they fulfilled; he grants that the finishing came fifty years before Longimanus reigned, and infers from his being the only one styled king of Persia that Ezra is writing in his reign and has added the name to the original record. Clarke turns the list into a chronology of favour, God giving the first order and stirring up each king after to second it, from Cyrus through Darius Hystaspes to Longimanus, who sent Ezra with new privileges, and the permission under which Nehemiah came. Wesley supplies the caution: the success was not to be put down to chance or to Darius's good humour, but to God, who required the work by his prophets and disposed the king's heart.

At the dedication the twelve goats carry the weight. Gill calls the hundred bullocks, two hundred rams and four hundred lambs hecatombs of various sorts, grand sacrifices even by heathen reckoning and such as Homer speaks of, and distinguishes the burnt offerings from the peace offerings, part of which fell to the offerers to feast on with gladness. Clarke says shortly that the he-goats were a sin offering for every tribe. Ellicott presses why: the worshippers are no longer Judah, nor Judah and Benjamin, but all Israel, and though the kid was the standing sin offering at the atonement, the new moons and the great feasts, only here is one brought for each tribe. Delitzsch agrees that the number answers to the tribes because the temple was meant for the whole covenant people, whose return the prophets had taught them to hope for, and expressly rejects the older explanation that families of the ten tribes already settled in Judah were among them, the sense Gill gives to the children of Israel here. On the ministry Gill has the priests and Levites set in their proper classes to serve in turn, and Delitzsch the same, each class in its week; Ellicott warns that only the general arrangements stood in the law, the courses being of David's time, and that the restoration must have been imperfect, with neither the priestly courses complete nor the Levites in full force. Clarke marks the seam: with this verse the Aramaic part of the chapter ends.
19:
The Passover falls close on the dedication, and the sources mark both the nearness and the exactness. Gill names the month Nisan or Abib, the one after that in which the house was finished, and notes that the feast was kept at the precise time the law commanded. Delitzsch counts only a few weeks between the two, and reads the reason given as an explanation of possibility: the congregation could keep and eat the Passover because the priests had purified themselves and were fit to sprinkle the blood, and the Levites were clean as well. Ellicott notices a change of another kind: in recording this celebration, after the precedent of two earlier reforming kings, Ezra returns to Hebrew, and he reads the occasion as a renewal of the redemption from Egypt, another wilderness having been passed. All three measure the purity of the ministers against the best previous attempt and find it better. Gill has them pure to a man and purified as one man, all of one mind and as quick about it as if a single man had been in question.

Clarke makes the point from the law instead: because all were ready at one time, there was no need of the second Passover appointed for those accidentally defiled or absent from the tabernacle. Ellicott gets the same sense by repunctuating against the received accentuation, so that the priests were purified, the Levites were purified as one man, all were pure, and killed; and he adds that the purity of both orders here surpassed the earlier celebration, and that the Levites had by now come to slaughter all the paschal lambs. On who then ate the Passover the sources divide sharply. Clarke takes those who had separated themselves to be proselytes, gentiles who had embraced the Jewish religion through mixing with the captives, and draws the moral that the poor exiles had so acted on their principles that the heathen saw it and walked in the light of the Lord with them, a good example being persuasive when founded on pure principles. Ellicott denies it outright: not proselytes from the heathen are intended, but the remnant of Jews left in the land who had consorted with the populations the conquerors introduced, whose intermarriages and other conformities these books refer to constantly.

On the returned company itself Gill sees Judah and Benjamin with some of the ten tribes mixed among them, while Wesley thinks probably some out of each of the twelve. The feast of unleavened bread follows immediately, as Gill notes, and Ellicott reads it as the symbol of entire separation from evil to the service of the God whom at the Passover they had taken for their own. Its particular joy, he says, lay in the sense that the Lord had turned the heart of the king, who is styled king of Assyria as a remembrancer of what their oppressors had been. Every voice stops at that title. Delitzsch identifies him as Darius, so designated because he ruled the former realm of Assyria, and locates the turning of his heart in the strengthening of their hands, since by his goodwill they could finish the house and restore the worship of the God of Israel. Clarke follows Calmet in reading Assyria for Persia, since Cyrus and his successors held all the rights and estates of the old Assyrian kings, and adds what he knows of the man: a high character for wisdom, justice and mercy, a title strengthened by marrying two daughters of Cyrus, and so the readier to confirm their family's edict. Wesley keeps the emphasis theological: God gave them both cause to rejoice and hearts to rejoice, being himself the fountain from which all true joy flows, and the title is used pointedly, to mark the goodness of a God who turns the hearts of monarchs whose predecessors had been his people's chief persecutors.
